newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: U.N. envoy links aid to Afghan peace process.
newsitem.headline: U.N. envoy links aid to Afghan peace process.

text.p: U.N. special envoy Norbert Holl said on Tuesday that Afghan factions should understand that a link existed between aid flows and progress towards peace.

"Peace and stability are the indispensable aid that Afghanistan needs most at this time," Holl told a U.N.-organised international forum on assistance to Afghanistan that opened in the Turkmenistan capital Ashgabat on Tuesday.

A statement from his office in Islamabad quoted Holl as saying international goodwill and humanitarian resources were bound to be exhausted unless sustained by positive results on the political front.
He said aid levels were declining and international donors were increasingly making their contributions contingent on progress in the political negotiations.
"This link is an important point that the Afghan leaders, especially the warring sides, need to understand clearly for the benefit of the suffering Afghan people," he said.

"The people of Afghanistan, suffering from malnutrition, disease, lack of education and all the other evils of war, should not be taken hostage by the policy adopted by their leaders," the German diplomat said.
Holl brought representatives of the Islamic Taleban militia and a northern opposition alliance together for three days of talks that ended inconclusively in Islamabad last week.
The two sides agreed to meet again next month to discuss a ceasefire, an exchange of prisoners and other issues.
The next day the Taleban launched an assault north of Kabul, capturing Bagram military airbase and the town of Charikar.

On Monday the militia said it was ready for more talks with ethnic Uzbek leader General Abdul Rashid Dostum and former government commander Ahmad Shah Masood, but rejected a key opposition demand for the demilitarisation of Kabul.
Holl said that continued fighting north of Kabul, especially after the Taleban takeover of Kabul on September 27, had forced him to refocus on the urgent task of mediating a ceasefire.
He expressed disappointment that hostilities had resumed immediately after last week's Islamabad meeting and appealed for them to stop to enable renewed negotiations to take place.
Holl said that issues of human rights and gender equality in Afghanistan were important, but should be raised "prudently and not confrontationally" with the Afghan leaders concerned.
U.N. and other relief agencies have found it difficult to work under Taleban restrictions in the name of Islam that prevent most women from working or girls from going to school.

Holl said he hoped the Ashgabat meeting "will not only serve the legitimate goal of mobilising humanitarian aid for Afghanistan but perhaps more importantly serve to highlight the need for a sustained and durable political process".
